comments.text:
Two of my friends were rejected outright without receiving a single penny. One was denied on the grounds that his heart attack was caused by diabetes mellitus, which he had disclosed when purchasing the Care Supreme plan. In the other case, the company claimed that a urinary tract infection was a pre-existing disease. This is absurd because he had held the policy for two years—anyone with a serious, chronic urinary infection would not remain untreated for that long.

However, the first friend won his case in the Consumer Court, and the second has now filed his own case. The main point I want to highlight is that Care Insurance Company relies on the psychology that only a small number of people—maybe three or four out of a hundred—will actually go to court.

I would say that if someone has sufficient funds, it may be better to insure yourself financially to avoid mental stress. For example, if you have ₹5 lakh available, consider investing it in good mutual funds with advice from your financial consultant, and top it up regularly with at least the amount you would have paid as the annual policy premium. I have now done the same.

Care Insurance’s claim that your no-claim bonus will accumulate and turn ₹5 lakh into ₹10 lakh is misleading and mainly a marketing tactic. They keep increasing the premium every year until it becomes unaffordable. Instead of feeling cheated later, if you can arrange to invest ₹5 lakh in mutual funds, do that and insure yourself independently.
